faq.a: Repeated eosinophil‑mediated inflammation from parasitic infections leads to subendocardial fibrosis, which is endemic where those infections thrive.
faq.q: Why is EMF more common in tropical Africa?

faq.a: Early treatment of the trigger (e.g., anti‑helminthics) may halt progression, but established fibrosis is irreversible; surgery can improve symptoms in selected patients.
EMF shows thickened endocardium and apical obliteration, while constrictive pericarditis shows pericardial thickening and septal bounce without intraventricular fibrosis.
faq.q: What distinguishes EMF from constrictive pericarditis on echo?

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer from rural Tanzania presents with progressive peripheral edema and a history of recent helminth infection. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Perform bedside echocardiography to look for apical fibrosis and restrictive filling; it directly confirms EMF in this setting.
How does eosinophilia contribute to the pathogenesis of EMF? — Eosinophils release toxic granule proteins that damage endocardium, triggering fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.

A patient with EMF develops atrial fibrillation. Which drug class should be avoided and why? — Avoid non‑vitamin K oral anticoagulants that rely on renal clearance if renal function is unknown; prefer warfarin with INR monitoring.

What clinical feature helps you differentiate right‑sided EMF from isolated right‑sided constrictive pericarditis? — Presence of a palpable liver edge with ascites and a normal pericardial knock points to EMF; pericardial knock favors constriction.

When is surgical endocardial decortication indicated in EMF? — In Stage III disease with severe biventricular failure, refractory edema, and when imaging shows dense apical fibrosis amenable to resection.

Why might a normal peripheral eosinophil count mislead clinicians in a patient with established EMF? — Fibrosis persists after eosinophil levels normalize; reliance on eosinophilia alone can delay diagnosis.
Explain why ACE inhibitors are beneficial in EMF despite normal systolic function. — They reduce afterload and improve ventricular filling pressures, alleviating symptoms of restrictive physiology.

A patient cannot afford cardiac MRI. How would you proceed with diagnosis? — Use focused transthoracic echocardiography; if windows are poor, obtain a chest X‑ray and clinical assessment, and treat presumptively while arranging referral.
ai.title: Endomyocardial Fibrosis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Endomyocardial fibrosis (EMF) is a restrictive cardiomyopathy endemic to tropical Africa, caused by subendocardial fibrous thickening that obliterates ventricular apices. It presents with signs of right‑ or left‑sided heart failure and is linked to eosinophilia and chronic infections.

b: Diagnosis requires imaging (echocardiography or cardiac MRI) showing apical obliteration, thickened endocardium, and restrictive filling patterns.
Endomyocardial biopsy is rarely needed but confirms fibrosis if performed.
sections.p: EMF is a disease of the ventricular endocardium and subendocardial myocardium where dense fibrous tissue replaces normal myocardium, producing a restrictive physiology.

t.b: Does the heart have apical obliteration and restrictive filling? → Shows thickened endocardium, small ventricular cavity, bi‑atrial enlargement; confirms EMF.
Is there subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement? → Demonstrates fibrosis distribution; useful when echo windows are poor.
Is eosinophilia present? → Supports eosinophil‑mediated pathogenesis; normal count does not exclude EMF.
Are cardiac silhouette and pulmonary vasculature abnormal? → May show cardiomegaly, pulmonary congestion; nonspecific but guides further testing.

b: Stage I: Mild apical fibrosis, NYHA I‑II, preserved systolic function.
Stage II: Moderate fibrosis, NYHA III, signs of right‑sided failure.
Stage III: Extensive fibrosis, NYHA IV, severe biventricular failure.
sections.p: Staging follows the extent of apical involvement and functional class (NYHA).

b: Parasitic infections (e.g., helminths causing eosinophilia).
Chronic malaria or schistosomiasis with persistent inflammation.
HIV‑related immune dysregulation.
Tuberculosis myocarditis.
Herbal or traditional medicines with cardiotoxic compounds.
sections.p: EMF is multifactorial; in low‑resource tropical settings the leading associations are eosinophilia from parasitic infections and chronic inflammation.

b: Peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly (right‑sided).
Dyspnoea on exertion, orthopnoea, pulmonary crackles (left‑sided).
Jugular venous distension, hepato‑jugular reflux.
History of eosinophilia or recent parasitic infection.
sections.p: Patients develop progressive heart failure; right‑sided signs dominate when the right ventricle is involved, left‑sided when the left ventricle is affected.
Focus on imaging, eosinophil count, and exclusion of other restrictive cardiomyopathies.

t.b: Are there low voltage QRS or atrial enlargement? → May show nonspecific changes; helps rule out myocardial infarction.
Is heart failure present? → Elevated levels support clinical suspicion but are not disease‑specific.
Is eosinophilia (>500/µL) present? → Suggests eosinophil‑mediated injury; absence does not exclude EMF.
Is there pulmonary hypertension? → Helps assess severity of right‑sided failure.

b: Rapid progression to NYHA IV with refractory edema.
Pulmonary hypertension leading to right‑heart failure.
Thrombus formation in obliterated apices causing emboli.
Arrhythmias (atrial flutter/fibrillation).
sections.p: Complications arise from severe restriction and secondary pulmonary hypertension.

b: Treat parasitic infection with appropriate anti‑helminthic (e.g., albendazole).
Corticosteroids for acute eosinophilic myocarditis (short course).
Loop diuretics for volume overload; add aldosterone antagonist if persistent.
ACE inhibitor or ARB to reduce afterload and improve filling.
Beta‑blocker only if tachycardia persists and patient is euvolemic.
Refer for endocardial resection (surgical decortication) in Stage III when facilities exist.
sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger, relieve congestion, and prevent progression; surgery is limited to selected cases.

b: Clinic review every 3‑6 months with NYHA assessment.
Repeat echo annually or sooner if symptoms worsen.
Community de‑worming programs to reduce eosinophil‑driven disease.
Educate patients on avoiding unregulated herbal cardiotoxins.
sections.p: Regular clinical review and echocardiography monitor disease progression; primary prevention targets eosinophilia.

b: Left‑ventricular apical thrombus – lacks fibrous thickening on imaging.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy – shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy, not endocardial fibrosis.
Amyloidosis – systemic deposits, often with neuropathy; Congo‑red positive biopsy.
Chronic pericardial constriction – pericardial thickening, not intraventricular fibrosis.
sections.p: Conditions that also cause restrictive physiology or apical obliteration.

b: Normal ECG in early EMF; reliance on ECG alone can miss diagnosis.
Peripheral eosinophil count may normalize after infection resolves, yet fibrosis persists.
Chest X‑ray may show only mild cardiomegaly; absence of pulmonary congestion does not exclude severe restriction.
sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite advanced disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of dyspnoea or chest pain suggesting acute decompensation.
New onset syncope or severe hypotension.
Rapidly rising jugular venous pressure with cool extremities.
